description: Headline fact-sheet sidecar for the $100 Medicaid Dollars series. SEPARATE from ledger.json by design: the ledger answers 'how does $100 flow through the Sankey' and must conserve; this file answers 'what is notable about this jurisdiction' and is governed by a PROVENANCE contract, not a conservation one. Headlines may depart from the Sankey's basis as long as every value names its source, vintage, and basis. Do not force these to reconcile to the ledger.

derivation_values.ledger: Derives from the conserved ledger (auto-recomputed; cross-checked against ledger.json when present).
derivation_values.external: Pulled from an outside source on a different basis than the Sankey; cited, not reconciled.
derivation_values.modeled: An estimate derived by us from external anchors; must be visibly tagged as an estimate.

reconciliation_notes: Fact #3 (long-term care): the Sankey shows fee-for-service LTC (~30% of DC benefits, CMS-64 basis). The headline uses the comprehensive CMS/Mathematica LTSS measure that includes managed LTSS and PACE (~mid-to-high 30s%, national benchmark 33.5%). The difference is managed LTSS, which CMS-64 does not itemize. Both are correct on their own basis.

Fact #6 (leverage ratio) is the only ledger-derived headline: it is a function of the jurisdiction's blended federal share (FMAP). For a DC fork the ledger carries DC's 73.2% blended share, not the national 64.7%.
Fact #7 (H.R.1) is a modeled estimate, not a published DC-by-year figure. CBO/KFF publish 10-year totals; the year split is our derivation from the national ramp and is tagged 'modeled'.

custom_analysis_library.description: Menu of reusable analysis TYPES that do NOT port cleanly across jurisdictions. The question travels; the numbers and even the binding factors must be rebuilt per state. Each state's instances live under states.<CODE>.custom_analyses. When onboarding a state, copy the relevant type as a stub (status='stub') and fill it locally. Keeping these out of the shared 7-fact set is deliberate: the seven facts are the portable spine; this is where state idiosyncrasy lives.

types.title: Economic ripple of provider-spending cuts (tax base + health workforce)
types.question_template: If Medicaid provider spending falls ~<X>% by <YEAR>, how does that affect <STATE>'s own tax base and the employability of its health-care (incl. unionized) workforce?
types.why_not_portable: Hinges on jurisdiction-specific structure: state/local tax authority and treatment of non-resident income, the exempt share of the property base, commuting/leakage to neighbors, dominant payers and provider mix, LTC intensity, and union footprint. Both the magnitudes and the binding constraints differ enough that the analysis must be rebuilt, not scaled.
inputs_needed: provider-spending cut ($ and %) for the target year
state/local tax structure and treatment of non-resident wage income
exempt share of the property base; nonprofit-hospital footprint
resident vs. commuter split of the health workforce; regional leakage
IMPLAN run or scaled input-output multipliers

facts.headline: Nearly $5 billion a year.
facts.stat: DC Medicaid runs about $4.9 billion (FY2025) — roughly $3.6B federal, $1.3B local; about $4.44B of that buys actual health services.
facts.basis: DC executive budget: DHCF (agency HT0) gross funds, FY2025 approved. Higher than CMS-64 actuals (gross vs net; includes local-only Alliance/ICP and admin).
facts.source: DC OCFO, FY2025 Approved Budget — Dept. of Health Care Finance (HT0) tables; corroborated by DC Action.

facts.headline: Almost a quarter of the entire city budget.
facts.stat: At $4.9B of DC's $21.2 billion budget, about $1 of every $4.40 the District spends flows through its single largest agency.
facts.basis: DHCF gross funds ÷ total DC gross-funds budget, FY2025 approved (gross-to-gross).
facts.source: Congressional Research Service, DC FY2025 Budget Status (R48609); DC OCFO DHCF tables.

facts.headline: No state leans harder on long-term care.
facts.stat: LTC is about 30% of DC's Medicaid benefits on the fee-for-service lines alone — and higher counting the LTSS inside managed care and PACE — and DC spends more Medicaid LTSS per resident ($1,554) than any state in the country.
facts.basis: FFS share (~30%) is CMS-64/MACStats Ex.17 (Sankey-consistent floor). All-in LTSS share and per-resident rank use the comprehensive CMS/Mathematica LTSS measure incl. managed LTSS + PACE.
facts.source: MACStats Ex.17 (FFS LTSS, FY2024); CMS Medicaid LTSS Annual Expenditures Report (per-resident #1; national 33.5%), FY2020 — most recent comprehensive report.
facts.notes: Ledger-consistent alternative if you want a fully ledger-derived value: 'fee-for-service LTC is ~30% of benefits' with a footnote that managed LTSS pushes it higher.

facts.headline: Near-universal coverage — but the gap just doubled.
facts.stat: DC has one of the lowest uninsured rates in the country, yet it jumped from 2.7% to 4.5% in 2024 — the steepest one-year rise of any state — leaving about 95.5% of residents covered.
facts.basis: Census American Community Survey 1-year uninsured rate.
facts.source: U.S. Census Bureau ACS 2024 1-year estimates; SHADAC analysis.

facts.headline: More than one in three Washingtonians is on Medicaid.
facts.stat: About 257,000 residents — 38% (north of 300,000 counting the locally funded Alliance) — and Medicaid pays for 46% of all DC births.
facts.basis: KFF state Medicaid fact sheet (Medicaid + CHIP enrollment as share of population); births share per KFF/DC Action.
facts.source: KFF, 'Medicaid in the District of Columbia' (May 2025); enrollment incl. Alliance per healthinsurance.org.

facts.headline: For every local dollar, the federal government sends almost three — and the program delivers nearly four.
facts.stat: At DC's ~73% blended match, each $1.00 of care is about $0.73 federal and $0.27 local — roughly $2.70 federal : $1.00 local : $3.70 of care (and $1 local unlocks $9 federal for the 90%-matched expansion adults).
facts.basis: Function of DC's blended federal share (FMAP). Derives from the ledger; for a DC fork the ledger carries DC's 73.2% blended share (MACStats Ex.16: federal $3,199M / total $4,372M).
facts.source: MACStats Exhibit 16, Medicaid Spending by State, Category, and Source of Funds, FY2024 (DC line).

facts.headline: The bite deepens fast — about 1 in 25 of DC's Medicaid care dollars gone in 2027, 1 in 11 by 2028, 1 in 8 by 2029.
facts.stat: DC stands to lose roughly $175–235M of Medicaid-funded care in FY2027 (~4%), ~$400–540M in FY2028 (~9%), and ~$650–730M in FY2029 (~13%) — counted as total program dollars, since every lost federal dollar pulls DC's local match and provider revenue down with it. Work requirements and more frequent renewals hit first; provider-tax limits and payment caps pile on through 2028–29.
facts.basis: ESTIMATE, state perspective, CARE basis. Reduction measured against total DC Medicaid benefits (federal+state care dollars), ~$4.14B FY2024 grown ~5%/yr. Federal funding cut run through the national year-by-year ramp and provision timing, calibrated to the published full-phase anchor (national federal Medicaid -12.7% in 2029, Commonwealth Fund), then grossed up to care via DC's ~73.8% benefits federal share. DC's own KFF 10-year and CF 2029 rows live in chart/image appendices and should replace the scaled values when extracted. Excludes the separate, unpassed FMAP-recalculation threat (~$731M-$1.1B/yr).

value.basis_denominator: care = total DC Medicaid benefits (federal+state), ~$4.14B FY2024 grown ~5%/yr
value.key_identity: For coverage-driven cuts the percentage reduction is identical whether measured against federal funds or total care — federal and state dollars leave proportionally. Only the dollar figure is larger on a care basis.
value.care_vs_costshift_note: FY2027 is almost entirely coverage loss (care actually stops). FY2028-29 add provider-tax/SDP financing cuts: DC can absorb these with local dollars (cost shift, not a care cut) or pass them through as lower provider payments (care cut). CBO assumes states backfill ~half — so the high end of 2028-29 is 'no backfill', the low end is 'full backfill'.
value.swing_factor: DC provider-tax / state-directed-payment exposure relative to the new federal caps governs whether 2028+ lands at the high or low end.

facts.source: Commonwealth Fund (Ku et al.), H.R.1 funding cuts brief, Jun 2026 (2029 = -12.7% national, $90.9B; cumulative $904B by 2034); KFF state allocation of CBO estimates, Jul 2025; CBO P.L. 119-21; provision timing per Georgetown CCF, Urban Institute, Pew.

custom_analyses.title: Economic ripple: tax base & health-workforce effects of a ~13% provider cut (2029)
custom_analyses.question: If DC Medicaid provider spending falls ~13% by 2029, how does that hit DC's tax base and the employability of its health-union workforce?
custom_analyses.basis: Scaled from Commonwealth Fund national IMPLAN ratios (~$1.30 lost GDP and ~$0.10 lost state/local tax per $1 of federal Medicaid cut; ~half of job losses inside health care) applied to DC's ~$500M FY2029 federal cut / ~$650-730M provider-revenue cut, then adjusted for DC's tax and workforce structure. Order-of-magnitude, not a DC-specific IMPLAN run.

tax_base.adjusted_local_revenue_loss: low-to-mid tens of millions/yr, with much of the true damage exported to MD/VA
why_lower_and_exported: Home Rule Act bars DC from taxing non-resident wages; >60% of the DC workforce and ~2/3 of income earned in DC are non-resident (mostly MD/VA), so the income-tax channel is muted and lands on the suburbs.
>50% of DC property is tax-exempt and the major hospitals are nonprofit, so there is little property-tax base to erode.
The metro supply chain is regional, so indirect/induced losses leak across the borders.
tax_base.secondary_pressure: More uninsured residents -> more uncompensated care and more demand on the locally funded Alliance; distressed providers will seek local bailout dollars.
tax_base.irony: The same commuter-tax prohibition that drives DC's structural deficit also insulates its tax base from commuter health-job losses; but resident workers (Wards 5/7/8) are exactly whom DC taxes and serves.

health_workforce.jobs_at_risk: Order of several thousand across the DC economy, ~half in health care; a substantial share are commuters whose jobs and income-tax effects sit in MD/VA.
health_workforce.most_exposed: Long-term care (nursing homes, home care) - the most Medicaid-dependent sector and the most unionized low-wage segment, and DC is LTC-heavy. Then safety-net hospitals (Howard, Cedar Hill) and FQHCs (Unity Health Care, Mary's Center, Community of Hope).
health_workforce.union_footprint: 1199SEIU (hospitals, nursing homes, home care, clinics, pharmacies) plus the nurses' unions.
health_workforce.mechanism: Layoffs, unit closures, hiring freezes, hours/wage pressure (template: NewYork-Presbyterian cut ~1,000 workers incl. 121 1199SEIU caregivers + 65 nurses, closing units). Union contracts cushion individuals (seniority/bumping/severance) but positions still contract; lower-seniority and new entrants are hit hardest.
health_workforce.compounding: DC's CFO already projects ~40,000 lost federal jobs and a mild recession this decade; health care was the cushioning sector, so this cut removes the shock absorber in the same window.

findings.swing_factor: Whether DC backfills the provider-tax/SDP cuts with local dollars (protects jobs, deepens the budget hole) or lets them flow through as provider-revenue cuts (protects the budget, costs the jobs).

sources.name: Commonwealth Fund (Ku et al.), H.R.1 funding cuts brief — IMPLAN ratios
Brookings, DC statehood fiscal implications — non-resident income, structural deficit
Tax Foundation — federal law bars DC taxing non-resident income
